description: We're a team interested in AI, data, and software, working on Field Shift. We're exploring how NASA Earth observation data, local conditions, and crop information can help farmers make informed decisions about resilient crop rotations. We welcome people interested in environmental or agricultural problems, with skills in Earth science, agriculture, data analysis, AI/ML, visualisation, web development, UI/UX, or design.
summary:
ASTRATERRA is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers compare crop rotations for their own field. A farmer selects a field on a map, has the option to correct auto-filled soil data, enters their current crops and sets priorities such as saving water, soil health, profit or forage.

ASTRATERRA combines NASA POWER weather (2005–2025) and NASA SRTM elevation with soil maps, USDA crop history and FAO-56 crop science. It replays the current rotation and four alternatives through every past year, showing when crops ran short of water, which slopes erode, and when the soil lies bare during heavy-rain months. Each option comes with the reasons, evidence, benefits, data gaps and risks for local review, and every score traces back to a real number.

We checked the model against reality: using only NASA weather, its two worst drought years were the two lowest corn yields on USDA record for our Wisconsin demo county.

As weather becomes less predictable, farmers need evidence from their own fields. ASTRATERRA turns decades of NASA data into clear, field-specific choices that support farmer judgment.
details:
What it does

ASTRATERRA is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that protect their soil and hold up to changing weather. A farmer picks their field on a map or searches an address. They review soil values that are filled in automatically (correcting them or answering "I don't know"), and confirm their current crops, which are detected automatically from USDA satellite crop maps in the US. They set priorities (saving water, soil health, profit, forage) and the equipment they have. The app then compares the current rotation with four alternatives: a cereal rye cover crop, winter wheat with red clover, a two-year alfalfa phase, and a drought-tolerant sorghum option.

How it works

For the selected point, the backend fetches four sources in parallel and caches them:

  • NASA POWER: 21 years of daily weather (temperature, rain, solar radiation, humidity, root-zone soil wetness)
  • NASA SRTM: 30 m elevation
  • SoilGrids: soil texture, organic carbon and pH
  • USDA Cropland Data Layer: the field's crop history

Because these sources come at very different resolutions (about 50 km, 250 m and 30 m), we harmonise them to one field and aggregate daily data to months.

The core is an FAO-56 soil water balance. Crop water demand is reference evapotranspiration (Hargreaves) multiplied by crop coefficients built from each crop's planting window and growth stages. A soil "bucket", sized by soil texture (Saxton & Rawls) and root depth, holds the water. Every rotation is replayed through each year from 2005 to 2025, and farmers can click any year to see the soil water run dry month by month.

Key calculations

  • Crop water demand (mm/month) = reference evapotranspiration ET₀ (Hargreaves, FAO-56 eq. 52) × crop coefficient Kc for that month. Kc curves are built from each crop's planting window and FAO-56 growth stages.
  • Soil water the crop can use = plant-available water per metre of soil (from texture, Saxton & Rawls 2006) × the crop's effective root depth.
  • Each month: soil water + rain − water used. Above full capacity, the extra drains away; below 50% of capacity, the crop is stressed (FAO-56).
  • Season water stress = the share of the crop's water demand that was not met: under 15% is OK, 15–34% is stress, 35% or more is failed.
  • Fit score = weighted average of the score groups (water, soil health, profit, forage), using the farmer's priority sliders.

How each score was calculated (0-100, worst to best)

  • Saving water: average water shortfall over the 21 replayed years: 0% shortfall = 100, 30% or more = 0.
  • Soil health = average of five sub-scores:
  • Erosion protection: bare months weighted by how stormy each month is at this field (NASA POWER heavy-rain days), scaled by the field's slope (NASA SRTM).
    • Nitrogen: share of years with a nitrogen-fixing legume (main crop = full credit, legume cover crop = half).
    • Pest-cycle breaks: more different crops and plant families = higher score.
    • Organic matter: yearly residue and root value of each crop, plus a bonus for cover crops (heuristic indicator).

Elevation gives erosion-prone slopes and low spots where cold air can collect. K-means clustering groups the 21 summers into hot/dry, normal and wet/cool years, and Mann-Kendall tests check for long-term trends.

Rule-based scores are weighted by the farmer's priorities and turned into sentences:

  • The recommendation with its reasons and trade-offs
  • A breakdown of how the fit score is built
  • For each rotation: why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, data gaps and risks for local review

Every claim traces back to a number and its source. No AI model decides the scores; they come from documented rules.

A Farm Journal lets farmers log each season: crop, planting and harvest months, outcome and notes. USDA satellite records pre-fill past years. Simple rules spot patterns and suggest causes to check, such as failed crops that prefer a different soil pH, poor years that match the driest summers in the NASA record, or a crop following itself.

Validation

We compared the model with real USDA NASS county corn yields for Vernon County, Wisconsin (2005–2025). The model never sees the yields; it only uses NASA weather. Its two worst drought years for corn, 2012 and 2023, were the two lowest corn yields in the county record, both about 17% below trend. This is a first consistency check, not a yield forecast. Losses from flooding, hail or disease are outside the model's scope.

Benefits

  • Field-specific: the same rotation scores differently on a steep slope than on flat land.
  • Transparent: reasons, evidence, trade-offs and data gaps are shown for every option.
  • Fast and free: about 3 minutes, no account, public data only, and answers stay in the browser.

Intended impact

ASTRATERRA helps farmers explore rotations that improve soil health and resilience before committing a field for years, and gives them field-specific evidence to discuss with agronomists and extension agents. The core data (NASA POWER, SRTM, SoilGrids) is global.

Tools

Python (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, pymannkendall)

React, Vite and Leaflet (charts drawn with SVG)

GitHub

Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant; Cursor IDE

No hardware is needed; the app runs in any web browser.

Creativity

Instead of a dashboard of data layers, ASTRATERRA asks a concrete question: what would have happened to each rotation on this field over the last 21 years? Farmers can click any past year and watch the soil water run dry month by month. USDA satellite history pre-fills the farmer's own journal, linking NASA data with their own records

Factors we considered

  • Farmer-centred design: a guided flow, plain language, an optional survey and a printable report.
  • Scientific honesty: explainable rules, validation against real yields, and stated limits.
  • Transparency about data quality: water, erosion, bare-month, nitrogen and pest-break scores come from the model and a sourced crop database. Organic-matter and forage scores are labelled as heuristic indicators, and profit as a placeholder until local prices are added.
  • Local expertise: every option lists risks for local review.
  • Licensing and privacy: SoilGrids is credited under CC-BY 4.0, API limits are respected, and there is no login.
